#Question 1:
Compare m1 and m2 above. Both were built from 1:9 with nrow = 3, ncol = 3, but they look different.

Explain exactly what byrow = TRUE changes about how R fills a matrix.
```{r}
# Create m1 (filled column by column by default)
m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
print(m1)
```

```{r}
# Create m2 (filled row by row using byrow = TRUE)
m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
print(m2)
```
by default (byrow = FALSE), R fills matrices column by column (downwards first). Adding byrow = TRUE changes this behavior so that R fills the matrix row by row (across from left to right) instead.


#Question 2:
If you tried matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3) (only 8 numbers for 9 slots), what do you think would happen?

Test it and explain the result, including any warning message.

```{r}
# Test matrix with 8 numbers for 9 slots
matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
```
This warning sentence means that your 8 data points cannot be divided evenly across 3 rows, leaving 1 empty slot in the $3 \times 3$ matrix. To fill this missing 9th slot, R automatically recycles the first value (1) and throws this warning to alert you of the length mismatch.

#Question 3
```{r}
# Run class() to check the data structure
class(scores[1, ])
class(scores[, "Ben"])
```
When you extract a single row or column, R downgrades the data structure from a 2D matrix to a 1D vector. R does this automatically because a single row or column only has a single dimension of length, and vectors are the standard, simplified structure in R for storing a single sequence of uniform values.

#Question 4
In the matrix-logical chunk, the row/column names disappeared from your result. Why does subsetting with a logical condition (scores >= 90) lose the 2D shape and names that scores[1, ] kept?

Subsetting with a general condition like scores >= 90 checks every single item across the entire matrix and pulls out only the matching values, which can leave a different number of items per row or column. Because these extracted values no longer form a uniform rectangular grid, R strips away the 2D matrix shape and column/row names, flattening the result into a simple 1D vector.

#Question 5 a * b and a \%*\% b both “multiply” the same two matrices but give different results. Explain the difference between element-wise multiplication and matrix multiplication in your own words. 

Element-wise multiplication (*) multiplies each individual number in matrix a by the corresponding number in matrix b at the exact same position (e.g., top-left times top-left). 

Matrix multiplication (%*%) performs standard linear algebra dot-product multiplication, where rows are multiplied by columns to compute the new values.


#Question 6
t(scores) swaps rows and columns. Look at dim(scores) versus dim(scores_t). Why must the row/column names also swap positions when you transpose a matrix?

When you transpose a matrix using t(), the original rows completely become the new columns, and the original columns become the new rows. Because the entire 2D orientation flips, the row and column names must also swap positions so they stay correctly attached to their respective data values

#Question 7
What would happen if you tried cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100)) — giving 3 values for a matrix that only has 2 rows? Test it, read the warning/error, and explain why cbind() and rbind() require matching dimensions.
```{r}
# Test code:
cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100))
```

R will throw an error (or a warning depending on recycling rules, but typically a length mismatch error if it doesn't fit evenly) because scores only has 2 rows, but you provided a vector with 3 values. cbind() requires the number of rows in the new column to match the matrix's existing row count, and rbind() requires the number of columns to match the row width. This strict dimension requirement ensures that the resulting object maintains a valid, uniform rectangular grid.


#Question 8
In what situation would you use rbind() instead of cbind() when updating a dataset over time? Give a concrete example (e.g., daily sales, weekly attendance) and explain your reasoning.

You would use rbind() when your dataset grows by adding new observations or records over time, where each new entry represents a new row.

Concrete Example: Tracking daily sales for a coffee shop, where each column represents a metric (e.g., Revenue, Cups_Sold, Customer_Count) and each row represents a single day. As each new day passes, you append it to the bottom of the dataset as a new row using rbind(). By contrast, cbind() is used when adding entirely new variables or metrics (columns) for the existing subjects.

#Question 9
A matrix needs 2 indices (scores[row, col]) but an array needs 3 (arr[row, col, layer]). Using dim(arr), explain in your own words what each of the three numbers represents.

When you run dim(arr) and it returns 2 3 2, each number corresponds to a dimension of the array:

First number (2): The number of rows in each layer.
Second number (3): The number of columns in each layer.
Third number (2): The number of layers (or "slices") stacked together.


#Question 10
Give a real-world example of data that would naturally fit a 3D array structure (hint: think of something that has rows, columns, AND a third repeating dimension like time, subjects, or categories). Explain why a single 2D matrix would not be enough.

Real-World Example: Tracking daily weather data across different cities over multiple months.

Rows could represent meteorological metrics (e.g., Temperature, Humidity, Wind Speed).

Columns could represent specific cities (e.g., Iloilo, Manila, Cebu).

The third dimension (Layers) could represent different months of the year (e.g., January, February, March).

Why a 2D matrix is not enough: A 2D matrix is flat and can only handle two dimensions at once (like metrics vs. cities for a single month). If you want to compare multiple months or years of data without squishing everything together or losing your structured grid, you need a 3D array to add that third layer of depth.

#Question 11
Explain WHY you chose cbind() or rbind() in challenge-1. What clue in the data (shared row names vs. shared column names) told you which function was correct?

I chose rbind() because class_a and class_b contain different students (S1, S2 vs S3, S4) but share the exact same columns (Midterm, Final). Because we are adding more rows of students to the existing columns rather than adding new subjects/tests, rbind() is the correct function. The shared column names (Midterm and Final) were the key clue that the matrices needed to be stacked vertically.

#Question 12
Suppose instead of 2 classes you had 5 classes, each recorded as a separate matrix with the same 2 columns (Midterm, Final). Describe, in plain language (no code required), how you would combine all 5 into a single matrix, and how you would check your final result is correct using dim()?

How i combine: i would use rbind() to stack all 5 class matrices together into one large matrix (either by nesting rbind() calls or by putting them all into a list and using do.call(rbind, ...)). Since all 5 matrices share the same 2 columns (Midterm and Final), stacking them vertically adds all the students together under those same two score categories.

How to check with dim(): i would run dim() on your final combined matrix and verify that the number of columns is exactly 2, and that the number of rows equals the sum of all students across all 5 individual classes.


#Conclusion:
A matrix is a two-dimensional data structure restricted to rows and columns, whereas an array extends this concept into a third dimension (or more), functioning like multiple matrices stacked together as layers. While both store uniform data types, matrices are ideal for flat tabular datasets like grades or coordinates, whereas arrays are suited for multi-layered data like tracking metrics across different cities over multiple months.
